items.title: Dick Katz interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 7, 2002
items.q: including McCoy Tyner and Chick Corea

ctx.x: Is that because of all the tools they have available?

It’s the tools and it’s the culture. There is no emphasis on individuality anymore as a prized thing to strive for. Skills are it. Skills and versatility. I’m being — it’s a big assumption on my part but I would think that would go into many, many areas outside of music, in the corporate world and everything, there’s always a place — if the guy has got some real ideas, yeah, he’ll be all right. But the pressure to conform is very strong. The way they teach modal jazz, you learn your scales, yeah, and you find out…

have to know how to develop an idea. You may or may not involve modal harmony. I don’t think Miles sat around doing that when they made “Kind of Blue” you know? Bill Evans was a very intellectual musicians and he knew — yes he knew about that — but that wasn’t his whole thing. All right so —
